666.title: Removing grudges
666.hook: five ways to let go of a grudge: kindness, compassion, equanimity, not attending, remembering kamma
666.howItsDone: Buddhist teachers often give the five ways of removing resentment as practical advice for lay people and monastics alike, and many traditions pair it with loving-kindness meditation directed toward a difficult person.

segments.voice: Yesterday: the five remembrances, ending with heir to my deeds. Did you ask, before one choice, whether you'd like to inherit it? Today, a new week, and something nobody wants to inherit: a grudge. Day six hundred sixty-six.

A grudge can be big, or tiny: the coworker who took credit, the cousin who never paid back the forty dollars, the friend who didn't show up. Someone can be in the shower, thinking about nothing, and suddenly they're arguing with that person again. Winning, usually. A grudge is like a song stuck in your head that you didn't even like. The Book of Fives has a short, very practical sutta for exactly this. The Buddha gives the monks a toolkit, five tools, for when resentment rises toward anyone. Today: removing grudges.
screen: `SOMEONE NOT YET FORGIVEN.` → `ARGUING IN THE SHOWER.` → `A TOOLKIT OF FIVE.`

segments.voice: The Pali word for grudge here is aghata: resentment, ill will that keeps returning. The sutta says: when resentment arises toward someone, here are five ways to remove it. First, develop loving-kindness toward that person. Wish them well, on purpose, even if only a little. Second, if that's too much, develop compassion: see that they, too, are caught in suffering, maybe of their own making. Third, develop equanimity: steady, even-minded, not swinging toward them or away. Fourth, simply stop paying attention to them. Don't feed the thought. Let them go out of focus, the way you stop hearing the refrigerator hum. Fifth, apply kamma: this person is the owner of their deeds, heir to their deeds. Whatever they do, they will inherit. It's not your job to carry the bill. Notice what the list is not. It doesn't say the other person was right. It doesn't say pretend nothing happened. It doesn't even say make up with them. It's about removing the thing from your own mind, where it's doing the real damage. And notice there are five, not one. If kindness won't come, try compassion. If neither will come, try ignoring. Five tools leave room for the days when one won't work. Yesterday's line returns here, too: heir to my deeds. Today it's turned around: they are heirs to theirs.
screen: `KINDNESS, THEN COMPASSION.` · `EVEN-MINDEDNESS.` · `STOP FEEDING THE THOUGHT.` · then, large: `THEY ARE HEIRS TO THEIR DEEDS.`

segments.voice: Sit, and settle. Bring to mind the person, lightly, at a distance, as if across a street. Notice what rises in the body: heat, tightness, a story starting. Now pick one tool. Wish them well in a few words. Or see the suffering they're carrying. Or rest evenly, neither for nor against. Or, if it's too raw today, let them fade from focus and come back to the breath. Whichever you choose is the right one for now. The bell holds the time.
Removing grudges. Five tools from the Book of Fives: loving-kindness, compassion, equanimity, not paying attention, and remembering that each person is heir to their own deeds. Today's word.
Your line: grudge removed. Today, when the old argument starts up in your head, pick one of the five, and see how long the quiet lasts. Day six hundred sixty-six.

667.title: Food is life
667.hook: giving food gives life, beauty, happiness and strength
667.howItsDone: In Theravada countries, lay Buddhists offer food to monks on the morning alms round or at the temple, and giving food is one of the ways lay Buddhists practice dana, generosity.

segments.voice: Yesterday: removing grudges, five tools, and your line, grudge removed. Did one of the five quiet an old argument? Today, a gift that is easy to give without noticing. Day six hundred sixty-seven.

A Koliyan town called Sajjanela. A laywoman named Suppavasa has invited the Buddha to her house for a meal. She serves him with her own hands, good food, until he's had enough. Scenes like this one come up again and again in the suttas: a lay household inviting the Buddha for a meal. But this time, after the meal, the Buddha doesn't just thank her. He tells her what she has actually given. And it turns out a plate of rice is a bigger gift than it looks. Today: dana.
screen: `A LAYWOMAN NAMED SUPPAVASA.` → `SHE SERVES WITH HER OWN HANDS.` → `WHAT DID SHE REALLY GIVE?`

segments.voice: When a woman disciple gives food, the Buddha tells Suppavasa, she gives four things to the one who receives it. She gives life. She gives beauty. She gives happiness. She gives strength. Think about that literally. Without food, there's no life. Food puts color back in a pale face. A good meal after a long day is happiness you can taste. And it's what lets the body walk, work and sit in meditation. Then the second half, which is the surprise. Having given life, beauty, happiness and strength, the Buddha says, she herself will share in life, beauty, happiness and strength, whether among humans or among the gods. The gift goes out and comes back. This is how the early texts think about giving, dana. It isn't only a moral duty or a fee for teaching. It's a circle. The monk could not survive without the householder's food; the householder's giving becomes part of her own path. Notice, too, that the sutta is spoken to a woman, about a woman giver, and praises her by name. And notice what counts as the gift: not gold, not land. A meal. Something given, and received, every day.
screen: `SHE GIVES LIFE AND BEAUTY.` · `HAPPINESS AND STRENGTH.` · `THE GIFT COMES BACK.` · then, large: `FOOD IS LIFE.`

segments.voice: Sit, and settle for a few breaths. Bring to mind the last meal someone made or bought for you. Let yourself feel it again: life, color, comfort, strength. Now bring to mind someone you could feed today. A housemate, a coworker, a neighbor, a person on the corner, a food bank shelf. It doesn't need to be grand. A sandwich counts. A cup of tea counts. Picture handing it over, and the four things going with it. The bell holds the time.
dana. The Pali and Sanskrit word for giving, from the Buddha's words to Suppavasa: giving food gives life, beauty, happiness and strength, and the giver shares in all four. Today's word.
Your line: a gift that comes back. Today, feed one person on purpose, and as you hand it over, remember the four things you're giving. Day six hundred sixty-seven.

668.title: Pull your ears
668.hook: nodding Moggallana is given remedies for drowsiness: from pulling your ears to walking
668.howItsDone: Meditation teachers in many Buddhist traditions still give these remedies for sleepiness, such as opening the eyes, standing, or switching to walking meditation, and some retreats offer standing or walking periods for exactly this.

segments.voice: Yesterday: Suppavasa's meal, and your line, a gift that comes back. Who did you feed? Today, what happens after a good meal, when you sit down to meditate and your head starts to drop. Day six hundred sixty-eight.

The breath is slow, the room is warm, and then your chin dips toward your chest, and you jerk back up, hoping no one saw. Anyone who has sat to meditate knows that moment. In the Book of Sevens, it happens to Moggallana, one of the Buddha's two chief disciples, famous in the tradition for his powers of mind. He's sitting in meditation near a village in Magadha, and he keeps nodding. The Buddha, the text says, sees it from far away, and comes to him with a list of remedies. Today: pacala.
screen: `THE CHIN DIPS.` → `EVEN MOGGALLANA NODDED.` → `A LIST OF REMEDIES.`

segments.voice: Are you nodding, Moggallana? the Buddha asks. Yes, sir. Then comes a ladder, each step tried only if the one before doesn't work. First: whatever thought you were on when drowsiness came, stop giving it attention. Second: if that fails, think over a teaching you've learned. Third: recite a teaching out loud, in detail. Fourth: pull both your earlobes and rub your limbs with your hands. Fifth: get up, wash your eyes with water, and look around in every direction, and up at the stars. Sixth: bring to mind the perception of light, the idea of daytime, day and night alike. Seventh: walk up and down, with your senses gathered in. And if none of that works? Eighth: lie down on your right side, like a lion, mindful, with the thought of getting up again, and when you wake, get up promptly. Notice how practical this is. No one is scolded. Sleepiness isn't treated as a sin, just as a state with causes and cures. Thinking, then talking, then the body, then cold water and open sky, then movement, and last of all, permission to rest. The order matters. Most of us skip straight to the last step, or fight the first one forever. And then the sutta keeps going, with advice on pride and on argument. But the ear-pulling is the part people remember.
screen: `ARE YOU NODDING, MOGGALLANA?` · `THINK, RECITE, PULL YOUR EARS.` · `WATER, STARS, LIGHT, WALKING.` · then, large: `LAST OF ALL, REST.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: try one remedy. Sit up, and notice your level of alertness right now, honestly. If it's low, try the fourth step: gently take both earlobes between thumb and finger and give them a slow pull. Rub your hands together, then along your arms. Feel the body wake. If you're already alert, simply rest with the breath, and notice what alertness feels like, so you'll know it when it fades. The bell holds the time.

pacala. The Pali word for nodding or drowsiness, the state of Moggallana in the Book of Sevens, met by the Buddha with a ladder of remedies from changing the thought to looking at the stars. Today's word.
Your line: climb the ladder. Today, when the afternoon slump comes, climb the ladder: change the thought, splash water, look at the sky, walk. Day six hundred sixty-eight.

669.title: Eight winds
669.hook: gain and loss, fame and disrepute, praise and blame, pleasure and pain
669.howItsDone: Buddhist teachers in many traditions teach the eight worldly conditions as a check on daily life, and in East Asian Buddhism the 'eight winds' are a common image in sermons and poems about steadiness of mind.

segments.voice: Yesterday: drowsy Moggallana and your line, climb the ladder. Did you climb the ladder in the slump? Today, eight things that blow through every life, sleepy or awake. Day six hundred sixty-nine.

People in China tell a story about the poet Su Dongpo. He wrote a poem saying his meditation had grown so steady that the eight winds could not move him, and sent it across the river to his friend, a monk. The monk wrote one rude word on it and sent it back. The poet, furious, rowed straight over to complain. The monk laughed: eight winds can't move you, but one little puff blew you across the river. The story is legend. The eight winds are not. They come from a short sutta in the Book of Eights. Today: eight winds.
screen: `A POET'S PROUD POEM.` → `ONE RUDE WORD BACK.` → `ACROSS THE RIVER.`

segments.voice: In the Book of Eights, the Buddha says: these eight worldly conditions turn the world, and the world turns after them. Gain and loss. Fame and disrepute. Praise and blame. Pleasure and pain. Four pairs. One side of each pair we chase, the other we run from, and between the chasing and the running, a lot of life goes by. In Pali they're the lokadhamma, the ways of the world. The East Asian name, eight winds, is a good picture: they come and go, they push from different sides, and you don't choose the weather. Then, in the next discourse, he makes a sharp point. These eight come to everyone. To the person who hasn't heard the teaching, and to the noble disciple who has. So what's the difference? The untaught person, when gain comes, doesn't reflect: this is impermanent, painful, bound to change. So gain grabs their mind, and when loss comes, loss grabs it too. They're delighted, then crushed, and they don't get free. The taught disciple meets the same eight, and sees them for what they are. Gain doesn't take over the mind. Loss doesn't either. Notice: the disciple still gets praised and still gets blamed. Practice doesn't stop the weather. It changes how much the weather decides. That's the poet's joke, too. He was right about the eight winds, and wrong about himself.
screen: `FOUR PAIRS OF WINDS.` · `THEY COME TO EVERYONE.` · `ONE IS SWEPT AWAY.` · then, large: `ONE SEES THEM PASS.`

segments.voice: Sit, and let the breath settle. Then ask: which wind blew hardest on me today? A gain or a loss? Some praise, some blame? A pleasure, a pain? Name it, plainly, the way a forecaster names the weather. Feel where it lands in the body. Then just watch it, the way you'd watch wind move a tree. It came. It's moving. It will pass. The tree stays rooted. The bell holds the time.
Eight winds. Gain and loss, fame and disrepute, praise and blame, pleasure and pain: the eight worldly conditions that blow through every life. Today's word.
Your line: let the wind blow past. Today, when praise or blame comes your way, name the wind silently, and let it blow past. Day six hundred sixty-nine.

the eight come to everyone; the difference is whether they take over the mind.

the eight worldly conditions that turn the world.

it's a later Chinese story people tell; the eight conditions come from the sutta.

options: the disciple sees it as impermanent, and it doesn't take over the mind.
fork.reveal: the wind blows on both. the disciple sees it as impermanent and bound to change, so praise doesn't seize the mind, and blame doesn't either.

original.note: Pali lokadhamma: 'world-conditions,' the eight worldly conditions.

what it means: in AN 8.6 the eight winds blow on everyone; calm is not being carried off by them.

670.title: Householder happiness
670.hook: to Dighajanu: effort, protection, good friends, balanced living
670.howItsDone: Buddhist teachers often cite the Dighajanu Sutta, sometimes called the Vyagghapajja Sutta, when speaking about work, money and family life, as the Buddha's counsel for lay people.

segments.voice: Yesterday: the eight winds, gain and loss among them, and your line, let the wind blow past. Which wind blew on you? Today, a man asks the Buddha a question about gain and loss of the most practical kind: money. Day six hundred seventy.

Dighajanu is a layman of the Koliyan people, and he's honest about his situation. We're householders, he tells the Buddha. We live with wives and children, we use sandalwood, we wear garlands, we handle gold and silver. Teach us something that will bring us happiness in this life, and in the next. He isn't asking how to leave the world. He's asking how to live in it well. And the Buddha, whom people sometimes imagine as a teacher of monks only, gives him a plain, practical answer, starting with work and money. Today: householder happiness.
screen: `A LAYMAN NAMED DIGHAJANU.` → `WIVES, CHILDREN, GOLD.` → `HOW DO WE LIVE WELL?`

segments.voice: For happiness in this life, the Buddha says, four things. First, effort: being skilled and diligent in your work, whether farming, trading, herding or serving the king. Second, protection: guarding what you've honestly earned, so that it isn't lost to theft, fire, flood or careless heirs. Third, good friends: spending time with people who are wise, generous and steady, and learning from them. Fourth, balanced living. This one comes with a picture. A goldsmith, or his apprentice, holds up a pair of scales and knows: this much has tipped it down, this much has tipped it up. In the same way, a householder knows what comes in and what goes out, and lives so that income exceeds spending, but not by hoarding. The sutta even names both errors. Live too lavishly, and people say you're eating your wealth like a fig-eater; the old commentary pictures someone shaking a fig tree, knocking most of the fruit to the ground to eat a few. Live too stingily, and they say you'll die like a starving man. Then it names four drains on a fortune: chasing other people's spouses, drinking, gambling, and bad friends. And then, the other half of the sutta. For happiness in the next life, four more: faith, virtue, generosity and wisdom. Those may sound familiar. They're the same four that kept Nakula's parents together. The money advice and the spiritual advice sit in one discourse, side by side, like the two pans of the scale.
screen: `EFFORT IN YOUR WORK.` · `PROTECT WHAT YOU EARN.` · `GOOD FRIENDS.` · then, large: `BALANCED LIVING.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: balance one account. Sit, and settle. Picture the goldsmith's scale, two pans, a little needle in the middle. Now bring to mind one account in your life. It might be money. It might be time, or energy, or attention. What's coming in? What's going out? Which way is the needle leaning? No judgment, just reading the scale. Then imagine one small adjustment, a grain added here, a grain taken there, and feel the needle settle toward the middle. The bell holds the time.
Householder happiness. The Buddha's four for this life, effort, protection, good friends and balanced living, and four for the next: faith, virtue, generosity, wisdom. Today's word.
Your line: balanced living. Today, before one purchase, picture the goldsmith's scale, and ask which way this tips it. Day six hundred seventy.

trapdoor: what you thought: Buddhism only cares about giving things up.
what it means: the Buddha told a family man how to earn, protect and balance his wealth.
what a scholar hears: the man's name, Dighajanu, means 'long-knee'; the sutta is also called Vyagghapajja, after his clan's name.

671.title: Toward less
671.hook: to Mahapajapati: what leads to less, not more, is the teaching
671.howItsDone: Buddhist teachers often quote the brief teaching to Mahapajapati as a test for any practice or idea, and in the Theravada forest tradition 'wanting little' and contentment are held up as everyday monastic virtues.

segments.voice: Yesterday: householder happiness, the goldsmith's scale, and your line, balanced living. Which way did your scale tip? Today, a test for telling the teaching from anything else. Day six hundred seventy-one.

Mahapajapati Gotami was the Buddha's aunt. Tradition says that after his mother died she raised him as her own son, and that years later she was the first woman ordained as a nun, leading the women who followed her. In this sutta she comes to the Buddha with a short request. Please teach me the Dhamma in brief, so that having heard it, I can go and live alone, diligent and resolute. Not a long discourse. A rule of thumb she can carry into solitude. What he gives her is a test she can apply to anything. Today: toward less.
screen: `THE BUDDHA'S AUNT.` → `A NUN, ABOUT TO GO ALONE.` → `TEACH ME IN BRIEF.`

segments.voice: Gotami, the Buddha says, whatever things you know lead to passion, not to dispassion; to bondage, not to release; to piling up, not to letting go; to wanting much, not wanting little; to discontent, not contentment; to crowding together, not solitude; to laziness, not energy; to being a burden, not being easy to support: of those you can be sure, this is not the Dhamma, not the discipline, not the teacher's instruction. And the reverse. Whatever leads to dispassion, release, letting go, wanting little, contentment, solitude, energy and being easy to support: of that you can be sure, this is the Dhamma. Eight pairs, and they all point the same direction. Notice what he didn't give her. Not a list of doctrines to check. Not an authority to obey. A test by results. Look at where a thing leads. If it leads toward more, more grasping, more crowding, more needing, be careful. If it leads toward less, it's the way. That's why it's so portable. Gotami can take it into the forest and use it on anything: a habit, a friendship, a teacher's advice, even a meditation practice. The test is also gentle. Toward less doesn't mean nothing. It means the direction of travel. A little less wanting than yesterday is already the path. Put it next to yesterday's goldsmith: balance for the household, and for a nun heading into solitude, the needle tilting toward less.
screen: `TEACH ME IN BRIEF.` · `WHERE DOES IT LEAD?` · `MORE IS NOT THE WAY.` · then, large: `TOWARD LESS IS THE TEACHING.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: check one urge toward more. Sit, and settle. Let an urge come to mind, one from today or one that comes back often: another scroll, another snack, another purchase, another opinion. Don't push it away. Just ask the Buddha's question: where does this lead? Toward more wanting, or less? Toward contentment, or discontent? Feel the answer in the body. Then breathe out slowly, and imagine taking one small step toward less. The bell holds the time.
Toward less. The Buddha's brief teaching to Mahapajapati Gotami: whatever leads to letting go, wanting little and contentment, that is the Dhamma. Today's word.
Your line: where does this lead? Today, when you reach for more of something, pause and ask where it leads. Once is enough. Day six hundred seventy-one.

tradition says so: she was his aunt and became his foster mother.

fork.setup: you're Mahapajapati, about to live alone. you ask for a teaching in brief. what do you get?
options: a test: what leads toward less is the Dhamma.

fork.reveal: a test you can carry anywhere: look at where a thing leads. toward letting go and wanting little, it's the teaching; toward more, it isn't.

trapdoor: what you thought: you know a true teaching by who says it.

what a scholar hears: the eight are pairs of Pali words, like mahicchata and appicchata, wanting much and wanting little; the test judges a teaching by its fruit, not its source.

672.title: Sleep in peace
672.hook: the eleven blessings of metta, read whole
672.howItsDone: In some Theravada communities the eleven blessings of metta are chanted in Pali, and metta meditation, wishing well to oneself and then widening circles of beings, is a common practice before sleep.

segments.voice: Yesterday: Mahapajapati's brief teaching, and your line, where does this lead?. Did you catch one urge toward more? Today closes the week, and it ends, fittingly, at bedtime. Day six hundred seventy-two.

This week was full of tools for ordinary life. Five ways to remove a grudge. Food that gives life. Pulling your ears when you nod off. The eight winds. The goldsmith's scale. And toward less. Now the last sutta of the week, from the final book of the Numbered Sayings, the Book of Elevens. It's a list of what happens to a person who practices loving-kindness, metta, steadily: developed, cultivated, made a vehicle and a foundation, the text says, well established and well undertaken. There are eleven blessings, and today we read the whole list. Today: metta.
screen: `A WEEK OF TOOLS.` → `THE BOOK OF ELEVENS.` → `ELEVEN BLESSINGS, WHOLE.`

segments.voice: Here they are, in order. One: you sleep easily. Two: you wake easily. Three: you don't have bad dreams. Four: you are dear to human beings. Five: you are dear to non-human beings. Six: the devas, the gods, protect you. Seven: fire, poison and weapons don't touch you. Eight: your mind becomes concentrated quickly. Nine: your face is bright and clear. Ten: you die unconfused. Eleven: if you go no further in this life, you are reborn in the Brahma world. Notice where the list starts. Not with heaven. With sleep. The first three blessings are about the night, the place where resentment and worry do their best work, replaying the day at two in the morning. A heart that's practiced goodwill has less to replay. Then the list moves outward, to people, to unseen beings, to protection; then inward, to concentration and a clear face; and finally to the very end, dying without confusion. It's a whole life, from tonight's pillow to the last breath. Some of the blessings, like fire and poison not touching you, are read by some teachers literally, as the power of a mind full of kindness, and by others as describing a life that makes fewer enemies. The text itself simply lists them. And notice how this ties the week together. Grudges removed, winds passing, less wanting: all of it makes for a quieter night.
screen: `SLEEP EASY, WAKE EASY.` · `DEAR TO HUMANS AND NON-HUMANS.` · `A QUICK MIND, A BRIGHT FACE.` · then, large: `DIE UNCONFUSED.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: offer metta before sleep. You can do it now, or save it for your pillow tonight. Breathe slowly. Bring to mind yourself, and wish yourself well, in a few simple words: may I be well, may I rest. Then someone you love. Then someone neutral, a face you passed today. Then, if you can, someone from this week's grudges. Then everyone, everywhere, going to sleep tonight. Let the words get softer as you go. The bell holds the time.
metta. The Pali word for loving-kindness, the practice behind the eleven blessings in the Book of Elevens, a list that runs from an easy night to an unconfused death and beyond. Today's word.
Your line: wish one person well. Tonight, as you lie down, wish one person well, then yourself, and let that be the last thought of the day. Day six hundred seventy-two.

myth: the list of metta's blessings begins with heaven
it begins with sleep: sleeping easily, waking easily, no bad dreams.
there are eleven blessings in the list
it's in the Book of Elevens, the last book of the Numbered Sayings.
one blessing is being dear to non-human beings
dear to humans, and dear to non-humans too.

fork.setup: of the eleven blessings of metta, which comes first in the list?
fork.reveal: sleep comes first. the list starts with tonight's pillow and ends with dying unconfused.

original.note: Pali metta: loving-kindness, goodwill; from mitta, friend. Sanskrit maitri.

trapdoor: what you thought: loving-kindness is a nice feeling with no practical effect.
what it means: AN 11.16 lists eleven blessings, starting with sleep and ending with death.
what a scholar hears: the list is introduced with a stack of verbs, developed, cultivated, made a vehicle and a basis, to show it describes steady practice, not a passing mood.
